opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question. My time at DeepMind was really eye-opening. It's an incredible place: you have enormous compute, brilliant colleagues, and the freedom to work on very ambitious, long-horizon problems. Being in that environment showed me what's possible when you put a lot of resources and talent behind a single, focused research agenda.

But it also helped me understand what I personally wanted from my career. In industry labs, even very research-oriented ones, the direction is often shaped by the organization's priorities. That's not a bad thing; it's how you get big, coordinated efforts done. But I realized I really valued being able to set my own research agenda, especially in robotics, where I think a lot of the important questions are still wide open and don't always align with what's strategically convenient for a company at a given moment.

The other big factor was people. At DeepMind I worked with interns and junior researchers, and those were some of my favorite moments, seeing someone go from "I'm not sure what to work on" to having real ownership of an idea. Academia lets you do that at a much deeper level. You build a lab, train PhD students over five or six years, and watch them become independent researchers. That kind of long-term impact through people felt really meaningful to me.

So I'd say DeepMind didn't push me away from industry. It clarified what I cared about most: intellectual freedom, working on the foundational problems I believe in, and mentoring the next generation. A faculty position was the best way to bring all of those together. And honestly, the connections and perspective I gained there still shape how I run my lab today. I try to bring some of that ambition and collaborative spirit into an academic setting.

r001.rationale: The response says DeepMind clarified his priorities and describes the experience positively; it does not say he disliked the environment or that an internship solidified his decision.

r002.rationale: It says industry research direction is often shaped by organizational priorities, but does not describe DeepMind’s environment shifting from open, exploratory research toward top-down direction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, the honest answer is that my time at DeepMind was wonderful in a lot of ways, and that's partly why it clarified things for me. I was working with incredibly talented people, the compute and infrastructure were on a different level from anything I'd had as a PhD student at Stanford, and the research culture was genuinely serious. If you want to push on a big technical problem with a team, it's hard to imagine a better setup.

But a couple of things stood out to me over time. One was the question of who sets the agenda. In an industry lab, even a very research-oriented one, the questions you work on are shaped by organizational priorities. That's not a criticism, it's just the nature of the place. And I realized that what I cared most about was being able to pick problems that I thought were important for the long arc of robot learning, even if they didn't map cleanly onto a product direction or a flagship result. I wanted the freedom to be wrong in my own way, if that makes sense.

The second thing was mentorship. At DeepMind I got to work alongside interns and junior researchers, and I found that I really loved that part of the job. Watching someone go from having a vague idea to running a real experiment and understanding what the result means, that was often the most satisfying part of my week. In a faculty role, that's the core of what you do. You're building people as much as you're building systems.

And the last piece is that robotics specifically benefits from a certain kind of patience. A lot of the hard problems in manipulation, in learning from human demonstrations, in long-horizon planning, these don't resolve in a single quarter. Academia gives you room to sit with a problem for years, to let students take ownership of it, and to publish openly so the whole community can build on it. That openness mattered to me.

So I'd say DeepMind didn't push me away, it actually showed me what I valued by contrast. I came out of it knowing I wanted to run my own lab, work on problems I chose, and do it in a way where the primary output was both ideas and people. That's what led me to Georgia Tech.

What that experience helped me clarify was what I wanted from a research career. Being around people thinking deeply about ambitious problems was exciting, and that was something I wanted to carry forward. But I was also drawn to the opportunity to build a research group and work closely with students—not just on solving a problem, but on learning how to choose the right questions.

So, for me, pursuing a faculty position was about combining those interests: doing long-term research and helping other people develop into independent researchers. It wasn’t a rejection of an industry research environment; it was a choice about the kind of role I wanted to grow into.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what I really valued about DeepMind was the opportunity to be around people thinking deeply about ambitious, long-term research questions. That helped me clarify what I wanted in my own research environment: strong collaborators, intellectual freedom, and room to pursue ideas that might take time to develop.

A faculty position appealed to me because it also offered the opportunity to mentor students and build a group. Beyond pursuing particular research questions, I wanted to help students develop their own judgment and find the problems they were excited about. So it was really about bringing those elements together—ambitious research and education.
